video.title: Fantasy Basketball Power Forward Tier Rankings [NBA]

summary: Josh Lloyd ranks power forward eligible players in nine tiers for fantasy drafts. He warns that tiers carry over badly to basketball because positions are fluid, and says the list should not be the basis of a draft. A main theme is that standard nine-cat rankings badly misvalue some players. He says Giannis Antetokounmpo and Paolo Banchero are undervalued by them, while Chet Holmgren and Mikal Bridges are overvalued. Giannis is alone in tier one and is a clear pick five, and Jayson Tatum is alone in tier two and fine at picks six to eight. He notes many players worth more in points leagues than category leagues, flags injury risk (Kawhi Leonard, Anthony Davis, Karl-Anthony Towns), and names value picks such as Brandon Ingram, Lauri Markkanen, Paul George, Pascal Siakam at Fantrax ADP, and John Collins.

rules.text: Tiers do not translate well from fantasy football or baseball to basketball. Basketball positions are fluid and players at the same position do very different things.
rules.quote: In basketball, the positions are a little bit more fluid, but also what the players do

rules.text: Do not use positional tiers as the basis of drafting.
rules.quote: do not use this as the basis of drafting. You see tiers, and there are things

rules.text: Straight nine-cat rankings are a bad way to value players. If a player needs a 50-spot adjustment to reflect his real value, the ranking system is wrong.
rules.quote: If you have to make adjustments that are 50 spots to get relative value of a player, then the ranking system is wrong

rules.text: A low nine-cat ranking can wrongly suggest a useful player belongs on the waiver wire or bench. Paolo Banchero is the example.
rules.quote: that would suggest to you that in a 10-man league, they are a player you leave on the waiver wire

rules.text: Yahoo ranks and ADPs can be skewed by points league value. Check which format a rank reflects before using it.
rules.quote: So, his ADP's and ranks you got to sort of work out what it is.

rules.text: A player joining a new team can have growing pains.
rules.quote: My only hesitation on it is that on a new team, there can be some growing pains.

rules.text: Players with heavy injury risk can be fine in roto leagues but should be pushed down in head-to-head formats. Kawhi Leonard is the example.
rules.quote: In a roto league, if you want to do round three, go for it. But in any head-to-head format

rules.text: Teams coming off long playoff or championship runs may be cautious with their main players' minutes the next season.
rules.quote: I'm a little bit worried they just be somewhat cautious on him. Like they were with all of their main guys

rules.text: Rookies are usually drafted around pick 100 and play that way early, then improve as the season goes on.
rules.quote: like all rookies, I'm almost certain that he will be around pick 100 for the first 2 months

rules.text: A team that does not own its draft pick has less reason to fake injuries. But it may still give minutes to young players to see what they have.
rules.quote: Brooklyn being a team without their pick means that they don't have to avoid relegation zone.

rules.text: A big man moving from center to more power forward minutes usually loses field goal percentage, blocks and rebounds.
rules.quote: playing more power forward, as we know, means usually lower field goal percentage, lower blocks, lower rebounds.

rules.text: In the late rounds, hunt upside over stable low-upside players. Stable players are worth more in deeper leagues.
rules.quote: Stable enough to be your round 11 pick, but in a lot of cases, we want to hunt upside there

rules.text: Do not bank on a shooting improvement. Treat it as a bonus.
rules.quote: If he gets a shooting improvement, great. Just don't bank on it.

rules.text: Summer League three-point shooting numbers should not be trusted.
rules.quote: I think the three-point shooting numbers from Summer League are iffy and do not buy them
